title: Fake toll & DMV texts
summary: "You owe $6.99 in tolls" texts are the most reported scam text in the US right now.
how: Scammers send millions of texts claiming you owe a small toll, a DMV fee or a parking ticket. The link opens a convincing payment page that steals your card number, and sometimes your bank login.
spot: A small amount plus a big late fee or a 'license suspension' threat
A strange web address, often ending in .top, .xyz, .info or .cc
Sent from a foreign or random number, or an email address
You don't remember driving on a toll road
todo: Don't tap the link or reply
Check your balance by typing your toll agency's official website yourself
Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM), then delete it

title: Package delivery texts
summary: "Your package is on hold" texts steal card details with a tiny 'redelivery fee.'
how: You get a text or email saying a delivery failed, the address is incomplete, or customs needs a fee. The link leads to a fake carrier page that asks for a small payment, which is really a way to grab your card.
spot: You weren't expecting a package, or it doesn't name what you ordered
It asks for an address fix or a fee of a few dollars
The link isn't the carrier's real website
It came from an email address or overseas number
todo: Track packages only in the store's or carrier's official app
Never pay a 'redelivery' or 'customs' fee from a text
Forward it to 7726 and delete it

title: Fake bank fraud alerts
summary: "Your account is compromised" calls trick you into moving money to a 'safe account.'
how: A text about a large charge asks you to call a number, or a 'fraud agent' calls you. Caller ID may even show your bank's name. They say your money is in danger and walk you through sending it to a 'safe account' or reading them a code.
spot: Asks you to move money, buy gift cards or withdraw cash to 'protect' it
Asks for a one-time code, PIN or password
Tells you to lie to the bank teller
Creates panic and tells you not to hang up
todo: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card
Never move money to 'protect' it. Banks don't do that
Never share a code you receive by text

title: Grandparent & voice-clone calls
summary: A loved one 'in trouble' calls asking for bail money. AI can now copy their voice.
how: The caller pretends to be a grandchild or child in an emergency: an accident, an arrest, a hospital. A 'lawyer' or 'officer' may take over. With a few seconds of audio from social media, AI can make the voice sound real.
spot: An emergency that needs money right now
'Please don't tell Mom and Dad'
Payment by gift cards, cash by courier, wire or crypto
They avoid questions only the real person could answer
todo: Hang up and call your family member on their usual number
Agree on a family safe word and ask for it
Never hand cash to a 'courier'

title: Government & police impostors
summary: Fake tax, benefits, jury-duty or police calls threaten arrest unless you pay.
how: Callers claim to be from a tax office, a benefits agency, the court or the sheriff. They say there is a warrant, a suspended benefits number or unpaid taxes, and demand payment immediately.
spot: Threats of arrest, deportation or losing benefits
Demands payment by gift card, wire, crypto or cash
Robocalls that say 'press 1'
Asks you to confirm your Social Security number
todo: Hang up. Real agencies contact you by mail first
Look up the agency's official number yourself
Report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov

title: Tech-support pop-ups
summary: A loud warning says your computer is infected and to call a number. It's fake.
how: A web page or pop-up freezes your screen with alarms and a phone number. The 'technician' asks to connect to your computer, then 'finds' problems and charges you, or gets into your bank accounts.
spot: A pop-up with a phone number to call
Alarms, countdowns or 'do not close this window'
Asks to install a remote-access app
Fake refund 'mistakes' that you must pay back
todo: Close the browser. If it's stuck, restart the device
Never call a number from a pop-up
If you let someone in, disconnect from the internet and change your passwords from another device

title: Romance scams
summary: A sweet online love interest you've never met ends up needing money.
how: Scammers build a relationship over weeks or months on social media or dating apps. They're often 'overseas' as an engineer, soldier or doctor. Eventually there's an emergency, a customs fee or a ticket home that needs your money.
spot: Moves fast to words like 'love' and 'soulmate'
Can never video chat or meet in person
Asks for money, gift cards or crypto
Wants to move the chat to another app
todo: Never send money to someone you haven't met in person
Talk to a friend or family member about it
Report the profile on the app

title: Investment & 'pig-butchering'
summary: A friendly stranger teaches you to trade crypto. Your 'profits' are fake.
how: It often starts with a 'wrong number' text or a social media friend. They show off big profits and guide you to a trading site. The site shows huge gains, but when you try to withdraw, there are 'taxes' or 'fees' and the money is gone.
spot: Guaranteed or very high returns
A 'mentor' or 'VIP group' with secret tips
A trading app or site you've never heard of
You must pay a fee to withdraw
todo: Don't invest through someone you met online
Never pay to 'unlock' a withdrawal
Report it at ic3.gov

title: Job & task scams
summary: Easy money for 'liking' videos or rating products, until you have to pay in.
how: An unexpected text or DM offers remote work with big pay for simple tasks. At first you even get small payments. Then you're told to deposit your own money to unlock bigger tasks, or to cash a check and send part of it back.
spot: You were contacted out of the blue
High pay for little work, no interview
You must pay to get paid, or deposit a check and send money on
Chats move to Telegram or WhatsApp
todo: Never pay for a job
Don't deposit checks from strangers and send money back
Look up the company yourself and apply on its official site

title: Marketplace buyer & seller tricks
summary: QR codes, 'overpayments' and 'verification codes' empty your wallet.
how: On online marketplaces, fake buyers send QR codes or links to 'receive payment,' overpay and ask for a refund, or ask you to read back a code. Fake sellers ask for a deposit before you see the item.
spot: A buyer who won't meet and sends a courier
Links or QR codes to 'get paid'
Overpayment followed by a refund request
Asks you to read back a 6-digit code
todo: Meet in person in a public place and pay or get paid there
Use only the marketplace's built-in payment
Never share codes or scan a buyer's QR code

title: Prizes, lotteries & giveaways
summary: You 'won' something you never entered. Now pay a small fee to claim it.
how: A text, call or social media account says you've won a gift card, a phone or a sweepstakes. To claim it you must pay shipping, taxes or a fee, or share personal details.
spot: You never entered
A fee to receive a prize
A deadline like 'claim within 1 hour'
Copycat accounts with extra words like 'giveaway' or 'official'
todo: Real prizes are free. Never pay to win
Don't tap links in prize texts
Check the brand's official account directly

title: Phishing emails & fake invoices
summary: Look-alike emails want your password, or panic you with a fake charge.
how: Emails pretend to be from a streaming service, a shopping site, your email provider or your workplace. Some say your account is locked; others show a big charge and a number to 'cancel.' Both lead to scammers.
spot: The sender's address doesn't match the company
Spelling tricks like 'supp0rt' or extra words in the domain
Urgent buttons: 'Verify', 'Keep password', 'Cancel order'
An invoice for something you didn't buy
todo: Don't click. Open the company's app or type its address yourself
Check your real account or statement for the charge
Turn on two-step verification for your email
